answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.4.2024) The EU has developed and regularly updated a comprehensive set of policies that have allowed a decoupling of its economic activity, with a growth of gross domestic product (GDP) of 67% between 1990 and 20221, from greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, which declined by 32%2.

Eurostat reports that the total GDP growth in the EU in the last 15 years was 52%, 61% in Germany, 31% in Spain, 38% in France and 27% in Italy. The higher growth in the United States (US) can be influenced by a multitude of factors, including structural differences, innovation rates and demographics.

In its assessments of climate and energy policies, the Commission looks into the most costeffective solutions, building on the latest solid scientific insights, including the International Energy Agency (IEA)’s World Energy Outlook and Energy Technology Perspectives. The largest economies are accelerating their investment in the green transition.

The US Department of the Treasury assesses that the Inflation Reduction Act’s investment in clean technologies will be close to EUR 1 trillion3. China is adding more renewable energy than the rest of the globe combined: 2060 gigawatts (GW) expected in the period 2023-2028, compared to about 430 GW in the EU and 340 GW in the US4.

The Russian war of aggression against Ukraine and the following energy crisis have exposed the EU’s vulnerability to energy security of supply risks. The IEA assesses the EU avoids 180 billion cubic meters of gas imports every year due to clean technology deployment between 2019 and 20235. Thanks to gas demand reduction measures, the EU cut its gas consumption by more than 20% since 2021.
The EU’s climate and energy policies improves its energy security and protects consumers against even higher prices.
1 AMECO database. 2 Climate Action Progress Report 2023. 3 EEA (2024), EEA Report No 1/2024, European Climate Risk Assessment
